report:
**Conclusion:** Your “no” is too absolute. Olive leaf extract *may* lower blood pressure, but the evidence is limited and inconsistent—insufficient to regard it as a proven substitute for standard hypertension treatment.

**Evidence supporting an effect:** A 2022 systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized trials found beneficial blood-pressure effects overall, with larger apparent benefits in people who already had hypertension. However, included trials varied substantially in extract formulation, dose, duration, and study quality, so the pooled result is not definitive. [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9585795/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9585795/)

One relatively large, double-blind active-comparator trial in stage-1 hypertension reported that 500 mg twice daily of a standardized extract lowered systolic and diastolic pressure similarly to captopril over eight weeks. But it did **not** include a placebo group, was short, and equivalence to a drug in one study does not establish long-term effectiveness or cardiovascular-risk reduction. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/)

**Evidence against / uncertainty:** A randomized controlled study in overweight adults did not establish a consistent blood-pressure benefit, illustrating that effects may not generalize to people without established hypertension. [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8137474/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8137474/)

**Practical implication:** It is reasonable to say olive leaf extract is *promising but unproven*, not that it cannot work. Do not replace prescribed medication with it. It may add to the effect of blood-pressure medicines, potentially causing excessively low pressure; discuss it with a clinician or pharmacist first. [https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/olive-leaf](https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/olive-leaf)
